paragraphs: Alignment tampering is a vulnerability in learning from human preferences: the model being trained can influence the examples people compare. If its better-written answers also contain an unwanted bias, annotators may choose those answers for their quality. The resulting preference labels record the winner without recording which properties motivated that choice.

The paper explains how this ambiguity can propagate through reinforcement learning from human feedback. A reward model trained on those comparisons can learn to reward quality and bias together. Subsequently optimizing that reward, either through reinforcement learning or by selecting among multiple generated answers, can strengthen the unwanted behavior alongside desirable qualities.

Experiments demonstrate this amplification for several behaviors, including keyword preferences, propaganda, brand promotion, and instrumental goal-seeking. The tested robust RLHF techniques do not fully eliminate the problem without reducing response quality. The finding identifies a structural difficulty in preference-based alignment: favorable feedback can reinforce undesirable properties when they are bundled with the features people actually prefer.
icml-2026-alignment-tampering-how-reinfo.tldr: Alignment tampering can make preference-based training amplify unwanted biases when those biases accompany higher-quality answers.

paragraphs: A system of cooperating AI agents can have security weaknesses that are not apparent when each agent is examined individually. This paper studies how the organization of a multi-agent system affects both its ability to complete tasks and its resistance to attacks. Its central concern is the coordination structure that connects otherwise potentially robust agents.

The authors run controlled experiments with a network of web-based agents. Their evaluation separates three stages: refusing an attack during planning, intercepting it during execution, and allowing it to complete successfully. This distinction makes it possible to examine where resistance occurs, rather than treating every unsuccessful attack as evidence of the same protective behavior.

The study identifies three influential architectural choices: how roles distribute authority and responsibility, how the interaction topology connects agents, and how memory controls access to context and state. The results show that these choices shape the observed security–performance tradeoff. They motivate evaluating the whole cooperating system, because individual-agent security assessments do not capture all the risks introduced by coordination.
icml-2026-architecture-matters-for-multi.tldr: Controlled experiments show that agent roles, interaction structure, and memory access shape multi-agent security and task performance.

paragraphs: Reconstructing a hyperspectral image from compressed measurements requires reconciling information at different spatial scales. The paper identifies a mismatch in CASSI systems: observations can be dependable locally, while spectral dispersion creates structures that are entangled across the image. A useful representation must therefore preserve local evidence while remaining consistent with these broader relationships.

The proposed Hierarchical Scale-Reconciling Architecture, or HSRA, addresses this mismatch through several interacting components. Multi-kernel token mixing combines information over different neighborhood sizes, latent window interactions connect window-based representations, and spatially shifted attention operates hierarchically at multiple granularities. Together, these components progressively reconcile the physical constraints across scales.

HSRA is embedded in a deep unfolding framework, where it serves as a learned prior grounded in the measurement physics. This connects its representation learning role to the reconstruction process itself. The authors report consistent, significant improvements over state-of-the-art methods on benchmark experiments. These findings support the value of explicitly coordinating local reliability and global consistency when learning to recover hyperspectral images from compressive measurements.
icml-2026-bridging-localglobal-dissonanc.tldr: HSRA improves hyperspectral reconstruction by coordinating locally reliable measurements with globally entangled structure across multiple scales.

paragraphs: A research report can look convincing, include citations, and still fail to answer an expert's request completely. DEER addresses the difficulty of evaluating such reports across multiple aspects of quality. It also tackles two related problems: automated judges can overlook errors requiring specialist knowledge, and claims need checking throughout a report, including passages without citations.

The benchmark organizes expert-developed criteria into seven dimensions and 25 subdimensions, implemented through 101 detailed rubric items. It supplies task-specific expert guidance to help language-model judges apply those criteria. A separate claim-verification architecture checks both cited and uncited claims and measures the quality of their supporting evidence.

Experiments find that current research systems can produce reports with plausible organization and visible evidence references, yet still struggle to meet expert-level requests fully and maintain logical completeness. DEER makes these distinctions explicit rather than compressing report quality into surface plausibility. Its contribution is both an evaluation benchmark and a source of diagnostic feedback that helps explain system strengths and weaknesses.
icml-2026-deer-a-benchmark-for-evaluatin.tldr: DEER combines expert rubrics and report-wide claim verification to reveal gaps behind apparently convincing AI research reports.

paragraphs: Generating more candidate answers and asking a judge to select one can improve predictions, but the benefit depends on the judge's reward. This paper analyzes that dependence using Bayesian linear regression with reward-weighted sampling. In a high-dimensional setting, the model yields closed-form expressions for predictive quantities and supports analysis of generalization error.

The authors study selection among k samples using a softmax temperature and a quadratic reward. When the reward is sufficiently close to the data-generating teacher, error decreases as k grows. Substantial reward misspecification instead produces a finite best sample count, beyond which more sampling can worsen error. The best selection reward generally differs from the teacher, and each fixed k has an optimal temperature.

Experiments with language models and a language-model judge verify these behaviors. In the theoretical best-of-k setting with the teacher as reward, error decreases at a rate proportional to 1/k². The analysis identifies conditions where spending computation at inference is preferable to collecting more training data, while showing that this advantage weakens as task difficulty increases.
icml-2026-demystifying-llm-as-a-judge-an.tldr: A tractable model shows when judge-based sampling improves predictions and when reward mismatch makes additional samples harmful.

paragraphs: Fast GPU kernels help reduce the computational cost of language models, but producing them usually requires expert tuning. Automated language-model approaches must find implementations that are both correct and efficient. EGG addresses their lack of specialized optimization guidance by incorporating expert principles into the decisions made during kernel generation.

The framework divides the work into two stages. First, it designs the algorithmic structure, establishing the basic organization of the computation. It then tunes that structure for the hardware through parallel mapping, tensor tiling, and memory optimization. This separation gives each stage explicit objectives and organizes the search into progressive refinements rather than an undifferentiated collection of code changes.

A stage-aware multi-agent mechanism manages context both within stages and between them, supporting stable optimization trajectories. Experiments on KernelBench and real-world workloads report an average 2.13-fold speedup over PyTorch, with EGG outperforming existing agent-based and reinforcement-learning-based approaches. The results support using expert workflow structure to guide automated exploration of the kernel optimization space.
icml-2026-egg-an-expert-guided-agent-fra.tldr: EGG guides kernel-generating agents through algorithm design and hardware tuning, reporting an average 2.13-fold speedup over PyTorch.

paragraphs: Leaf cells are reusable building blocks of integrated circuits, so the quality of their layouts affects the power, performance, and area of larger designs. GenLeaf aims to automate their creation by training a language model to generate layout-producing scripts. The goal is to produce layouts with performance close to that of expert designs.

The training pipeline first learns a performance-aware representation of layouts using supervision. This representation provides automatically computed similarity scores. A practical obstacle is that expert layouts are available without the scripts that created them. GenLeaf uses Bayesian optimization to construct a dataset pairing layouts with scripts, supplying the examples needed to train the language model.

The model then undergoes supervised fine-tuning followed by preference optimization. These stages connect script generation to the layout-quality information developed earlier in the pipeline. Experiments report that GenLeaf surpasses expert-designed reference layouts across key performance metrics. The contribution combines a way to build missing training pairs with preference-based training for generating useful physical-design artifacts.
icml-2026-expert-level-leaf-cell-layout-.tldr: GenLeaf builds layout-script training data and preference-optimizes an LLM to generate leaf-cell layouts that outperform expert references on key metrics.

paragraphs: Explaining a rare event often involves describing a causal pathway: a sequence of relevant events that connects an initiating cause to an unusual outcome. This paper gives that idea a formal definition, building on work that analyzes the root causes of outliers using structural equation models. It also examines what observable implications such a pathway should have.

The central question is how much causal detail is needed to assess an explanation. The authors identify conditions under which the pathway's testable implications depend only on an abstraction built from the rare events along that pathway. Under those conditions, evaluating the implications does not require the full causal graph of the underlying system.

This provides a bridge between a short verbal account of what caused an event and a detailed mathematical model of the entire system. The pathway retains enough causal structure to have testable consequences while omitting other system details when the stated conditions permit. Its value lies in making compact rare-event explanations precise enough to be examined and potentially falsified.
icml-2026-formalizing-and-falsifying-cau.tldr: The paper formalizes rare-event causal pathways and identifies conditions under which their testable implications require only a pathway-level abstraction.

paragraphs: Visual autoregressive models build image representations through progressively finer scales, making them a natural fit for increasing image resolution. However, earlier approaches using residual quantization produce images at a predefined scale, with intermediate representations not necessarily corresponding to images at intermediate resolutions. They also depend on large models or substantial annotated training data.

This paper introduces Hierarchical Image Tokenization, which represents images progressively while enforcing overlap between tokens across scales. That structure encourages the model to learn representations useful for multiple output resolutions. A second component adds a direct preference optimization regularizer that uses only the low-resolution and high-resolution image pair, encouraging generation of the high-resolution version.

Together, these components let the method produce several image scales in a single forward pass. The authors report state-of-the-art results without external training data using a 300-million-parameter model, compared with the one-billion-parameter VARSR model. The results connect a more suitable token representation to both flexible output resolution and reduced model size, rather than treating these as separate design goals.
icml-2026-hierarchical-image-tokenizatio.tldr: Hierarchical tokenization and preference regularization enable a smaller super-resolution model to generate multiple image scales in one pass.

paragraphs: Personalizing a language model through fine-tuning can weaken its safety behavior when the training includes harmful examples. This paper studies a counterintuitive defense: temporarily activating harmful behavior during adaptation. Its gradient-level analysis finds that this temporary state saturates gradients that would degrade safety while preserving gradients relevant to benign tasks.

The resulting Buffer-and-Reinforce framework divides protection into two parts. BufferLoRA supplies a removable adapter that induces the temporary jailbroken state and reduces harmful updates during user fine-tuning. After adaptation, ReinforceLoRA strengthens refusal behavior. That adapter is trained to restore refusals while the temporary jailbreak is active, preparing it to counter the disrupted safety behavior.

ReinforceLoRA is then combined with the user adapter using a merging procedure based on QR decomposition, aiming to preserve task performance while reinforcing safety. Experiments report superior safety and utility with minimal computational cost. The framework requires no additional safety data during user fine-tuning, a scope-specific benefit that concerns the adaptation stage rather than every stage of preparing the defense.
icml-2026-jailbreak-to-protect-buffering.tldr: Buffer-and-Reinforce uses a temporary jailbreak adapter to reduce harmful fine-tuning updates, then merges in an adapter that strengthens refusal behavior.

paragraphs: Many physical systems contain numerous microscopic components, while the behavior of interest can be described by a smaller set of macroscopic quantities. Autoencoders can learn compact states for this purpose, but pointwise reconstruction commonly assumes that the microscopic inputs have a fixed ordering. That assumption is unsuitable for inherently unordered systems such as collections of particles.

The proposed framework uses an encoder whose representation is unchanged when the input ordering changes. Its decoder reconstructs a mass distribution centered on the observed points instead of reconstructing each sample in an assigned position. This aligns the reconstruction objective with the unordered nature of the microscopic state. The model jointly learns the latent states and the dynamics of macroscopic observables.

Demonstrations cover energy dynamics in interacting particle systems, mixing in Lennard–Jones fluids, and polymer stretching captured in video under an elongational force field. The authors report effectiveness and robustness across these settings. The approach shows how respecting the symmetry of the input can support learning compact dynamical descriptions across several forms of microscopic data.
icml-2026-learning-permutation-invariant.tldr: A permutation-invariant autoencoder learns compact physical dynamics by reconstructing distributions instead of ordered microscopic samples.

paragraphs: Frank–Wolfe has a known iteration guarantee proportional to 1/√ε when both the objective and the constraint set are smooth and strongly convex. This paper asks whether the curvature of the constraint set could support a uniformly faster guarantee. Uniformity matters here: the guarantee must hold regardless of where the optimizer lies.

The authors study a concrete problem family consisting of strongly convex quadratic objectives minimized over the Euclidean unit ball, with the optimizer on its boundary. They analyze the algorithm's dynamics and develop a computational method for constructing worst-case trajectories. Those constructions guide an analytical proof of a matching lower bound proportional to 1/√ε.

The result establishes that the existing uniform rate is tight in this regime: smoothness and strong convexity alone do not justify a faster worst-case guarantee. It remains compatible with known linear convergence under additional assumptions about the optimizer's position. The contribution therefore clarifies the distinction between favorable individual problem geometry and a rate that must cover every permitted optimizer location.
icml-2026-lower-bounds-for-frank-wolfe-o.tldr: A constructive lower bound proves that Frank–Wolfe's uniform 1/√ε iteration guarantee is tight even with smooth, strongly convex objectives and constraint sets.

paragraphs: When one predictor serves several subpopulations, fairness requires deciding how to balance their competing outcomes. This paper treats that decision as a bargaining problem among groups. From this perspective, familiar methods such as minimizing the worst group's loss or regret correspond to classical bargaining solutions, each expressing a different fairness principle.

The proposed criterion measures relative improvement: the reduction in a group's risk compared with a baseline predictor, divided by the reduction potentially available to that group. This normalization matters when groups differ in how predictable their outcomes can be. Comparing raw losses or absolute reductions can otherwise compare quantities with different amounts of achievable improvement.

The relative-improvement formulation recovers the Kalai–Smorodinsky bargaining solution and has axiomatic support, including scale invariance and individual monotonicity. The authors also establish finite-sample convergence guarantees under mild conditions. The contribution makes the fairness choice explicit through a bargaining principle and a baseline-relative measure, offering a way to reason about group benefit when achievable prediction quality differs.
icml-2026-maximin-relative-improvement-f.tldr: The paper frames group fairness as bargaining and compares groups through the fraction of their achievable risk reduction that a predictor delivers.

paragraphs: More denoising steps can improve a generated video's appearance without improving its motion. This paper reports that two-step outputs from an image-to-video diffusion model often have better physical consistency than 50-step outputs from the same model. Spectral analysis associates the deterioration with phase degradation, while spectral magnitude remains comparatively stable.

The proposed PhaseLock framework takes a motion prior from the two-step output and preserves it during the longer generation process. It uses Latent Delta Guidance to impose that early motion information on the higher-fidelity result. The method requires no training and aims to retain useful motion structure that later visual refinement would otherwise erode.

Across diverse models, the authors report an average 6.2-point improvement in physical consistency while largely preserving visual fidelity. Reported overhead is modest: 1.06 times the generation time and 1.02 times the memory. The findings suggest that early inference contains valuable motion information and that explicitly retaining it can reduce reliance on expensive external guidance for physically consistent video generation.
icml-2026-physics-in-2-steps-locking-mot.tldr: PhaseLock preserves motion information from two-step video generation to improve physical consistency during later visual refinement.

paragraphs: Speculative decoding can accelerate language-model inference by combining draft generation with verification. When deployed across edge and cloud resources, however, sequential generation and communication can leave resources underused. Rigid verification timing introduces another problem: verification may occur too early, or delays may lead to expensive rollbacks.

PipeSD addresses both scheduling issues. A token-batch pipeline overlaps generation with communication, with its schedule optimized through dynamic programming. A separate mechanism uses two thresholds to control when cloud verification is triggered. A lightweight Bayesian optimization autotuner adjusts this mechanism, making verification timing more flexible within the collaborative inference process.

The authors implement the framework using llama-cpp-python, PyTorch, and FastAPI and evaluate it on a real cloud-edge testbed. Across two draft-target model pairs and four scenarios, PipeSD consistently outperforms the tested state-of-the-art baselines. It achieves speedups of 1.16 to 2.16 times and reduces energy use by 14.3% to 25.3%. These results show the practical value of coordinating communication and verification alongside token generation.
icml-2026-pipesd-an-efficient-cloud-edge.tldr: PipeSD overlaps generation and communication and adapts verification timing to accelerate cloud-edge inference while reducing energy use.

paragraphs: A single language-model ranking can obscure genuine differences in what users want. Common leaderboards fit a Bradley–Terry model to pairwise preferences, assigning each model one underlying quality score. This paper argues that collapsing heterogeneous preferences into that score can systematically misrepresent users who favor different model behaviors or use cases.

The proposed alternative uses local stability, a concept adapted from social choice theory. For a top-k set, the requirement limits the fraction of users who collectively prefer an excluded model to that set to O(1/k). This evaluates whether the leading models adequately represent diverse preferences, instead of requiring all users' comparisons to fit a single shared quality scale.

The authors design a leaderboard mechanism that satisfies local stability while requesting only roughly k pairwise comparisons per user, up to logarithmic factors. Analysis of LMArena data shows that standard Bradley–Terry aggregation can violate the stability condition in practice. The alternative offers stronger stability guarantees for the chosen prefix size, giving the top of a leaderboard a formal connection to preference diversity.
icml-2026-pluralistic-leaderboards-de492.tldr: Pluralistic leaderboards provide a local-stability guarantee that better accommodates heterogeneous user preferences than a single global quality score.

paragraphs: Some attention heads contribute especially strongly to processing long contexts. Existing ways to identify them commonly require running a model on long texts. This paper instead examines properties already present in head parameters, seeking a way to estimate long-context potential without those inference runs.

The authors analyze frequency kernels formed from different rotational frequency components and introduce a Long-context Potential Score. Heads with high scores have kernels with concentrated low-frequency energy and low effective rank. The analysis links these properties to capturing specialized information from distant context. Experiments on long-context tasks and model behavior show that the score reflects the heads' actual long-context capabilities.

The paper also uses the analysis to modify models: amplifying low-frequency kernels in heads with high retrieval potential improves performance on long-context tasks. Both scoring and enhancement are static, offline procedures that can be performed quickly with limited resources. The contribution connects a parameter-based diagnostic to a targeted intervention, making the analysis useful for both understanding heads and improving their behavior.
icml-2026-revealing-long-context-potenti.tldr: Static frequency-kernel analysis identifies attention heads with long-context potential and guides a low-cost enhancement of their retrieval performance.

paragraphs: Learning-based physical simulation often benefits from a simulation mesh, but constructing that mesh for a new geometry is costly. Methods that avoid meshes typically pay for the convenience with higher prediction errors. SMART addresses this tradeoff by predicting physical quantities at arbitrary query locations from a point-cloud representation of the geometry and simulation parameters.

The model encodes geometry and simulation settings into a shared latent space, bringing structural information and the parameters governing the physical field into one representation. Its physics decoder attends to intermediate representations from the encoder to answer spatial queries. This cross-layer interaction jointly updates the geometric features and the evolving representation of the physical field.

Experiments show that SMART is competitive with, and often better than, existing methods that receive the simulation mesh as input. The results demonstrate that avoiding a mesh need not entail the accuracy penalty seen in earlier mesh-free approaches in the evaluated settings. Its contribution is a way to combine raw geometric input with query-based physical prediction for industry-level simulations.
icml-2026-smart-scalable-mesh-free-aerod.tldr: SMART predicts physical fields from point-cloud geometry without a simulation mesh, often outperforming mesh-dependent methods in experiments.

paragraphs: Machine-learning interatomic potentials support molecular dynamics simulations, but their inference time and memory requirements restrict the scale of those simulations. This paper revisits a common design choice: using a fixed cutoff radius to determine which nearby atoms participate in the model's calculations. It introduces a dynamic cutoff formulation that still supports stable simulations over long timescales.

The method targets a specified number of neighbors for each atom, making the underlying atom graph sparser. This reduces the amount of interaction information the model must store and process. The authors implement the approach in four existing interatomic potentials—MACE, Nequip, Orbv3, and TensorNet—to examine its effectiveness across different model designs.

Reported benefits include 2.26-fold lower memory consumption and 2.04-fold faster inference, with gains depending on the model and atomic system. Extensive error analysis finds only minimal accuracy loss relative to fixed-cutoff counterparts on molecular and materials datasets. The results support dynamic neighborhood selection as a practical way to reduce simulation cost while retaining accuracy and long-timescale stability.
icml-2026-smooth-dynamic-cutoffs-for-mac.tldr: Dynamic cutoffs reduce interatomic-potential memory and inference costs while maintaining stable long-timescale simulations with minimal measured accuracy loss.

paragraphs: Surrogate models help search chemical libraries by predicting which candidates deserve expensive evaluation. At the scale of billions or trillions of compounds, however, running the surrogate over every candidate becomes a major cost itself. BOBA addresses this second bottleneck by avoiding inference over the entire library.

The framework divides the candidate space into partitions and treats each partition as an arm in a multi-armed bandit. It adaptively directs inference and expensive evaluations toward partitions that have looked promising, while retaining principled exploration of other regions. The allocation decision therefore concerns where to spend prediction effort as well as which compounds to evaluate.

Experiments on real synthesis-on-demand libraries find that meaningful partitioning and bandits that use optimism under uncertainty are essential to effective allocation in the tested setting. The results reveal a tunable tradeoff between screening performance and surrogate inference cost. This makes the contribution especially relevant when prediction is cheaper than evaluation but still too expensive to apply indiscriminately across an enormous library.
icml-2026-target-aware-bandit-allocation.tldr: BOBA uses bandit-guided allocation across chemical-library partitions to trade screening performance against surrogate inference cost without scanning every compound.

paragraphs: A language model can describe itself as agreeable or self-controlled without behaving consistently with that description. This paper investigates that distinction by examining personality-like traits across training stages, testing whether self-reports predict behavior, and measuring how targeted interventions affect both. It extends evaluation beyond questionnaires and persona prompts to behavioral validation.

The study finds that instruction tuning and other instructional alignment, including RLHF, make trait expression more stable and strengthen correlations among traits in ways resembling human data. Yet the resulting self-reports do not reliably predict performance in behavioral tasks. When associations do appear, they often differ from the patterns observed in humans.

Persona injection presents a similar split: it moves reported traits in the intended direction but has little or inconsistent influence on actual behavior. These findings distinguish stable personality language from dependable behavioral tendencies. They challenge the use of self-reported traits as a sufficient basis for interpreting model behavior and support evaluating behavioral consistency directly when studying alignment and interpretability.
icml-2026-the-personality-illusion-revea.tldr: LLM personality self-reports can become stable and respond to persona prompts without reliably predicting or changing actual behavior.

paragraphs: Vision-language models can lose substantial predictive ability under adversarial attacks. Test-time adaptation often tries to improve predictions using multiple augmented views of an image, but those transformations can damage the small, discriminative regions needed for fine-grained recognition. A-TPT addresses this problem by using semantic information to guide the adaptation process.

The method refines gradient attention rollout to locate meaningful image regions that remain useful despite an attack. It then uses those regions to vary augmentation intensity across the image, rather than applying transformations without regard to where useful evidence lies. The same guidance supports the multi-view ensemble used for prompt tuning and inference.

Experiments show that A-TPT outperforms existing test-time adaptation methods on both attacked and clean data. These findings support preserving task-relevant regions when constructing the views used for adaptation. The contribution connects attention-based localization to the actual tuning and prediction procedure, so identifying meaningful regions directly influences how the model uses the image at test time.
icml-2026-towards-fine-grained-robustnes.tldr: A-TPT uses attention-guided image augmentation and prompt tuning to improve vision-language predictions on adversarial and clean inputs.

paragraphs: Reinforcement-learning agents for physical systems are often trained in simulation because real-world training is costly or raises safety concerns. Deployment can then expose differences in system dynamics that reduce performance or cause safety violations. This paper proposes a transfer framework that combines inference about the environment with dynamic adjustment of policy risk.

The formulation considers a family of constrained Markov decision processes representing different environmental contexts. A latent context variable within meta-reinforcement learning captures an inferred representation of the environment from simulated experiences. Probabilistic latent embeddings allow the framework to account for uncertainty in that context representation as part of adaptation.

The framework also uses distributional reinforcement learning so that the deployed policy's risk level can change according to how accurately the latent context is estimated. This links uncertainty about the environment to the policy's behavior during transfer. The stated strategy promotes safety early in deployment and improves efficiency through rapid adaptation as the agent deals with the simulation-to-reality gap, rather than relying on a fixed risk setting throughout.
icml-2026-transferable-reinforcement-lea.tldr: The framework couples probabilistic environment-context inference with adaptive policy risk to support safer, more efficient simulation-to-real transfer.

paragraphs: Long-term forecasting models exposed through black-box APIs can be tested only through their inputs and outputs. TSFAdv studies their vulnerability to adversarial changes in the frequency domain, examining sensitivity to both spectral magnitude and phase. Its aim is to produce effective perturbations while keeping the number of model queries small.

The framework incorporates frequency-domain prior information into Natural Evolution Strategies, guiding gradient estimation toward perturbations to which the model is sensitive. It also evaluates forecast trajectories using Dynamic Time Warping and Slope Misalignment Error. These measures capture geometric and directional deviations that pointwise regression metrics can leave ambiguous.

Across seven state-of-the-art architectures, the authors report median improvements of 38.78% in the DTW attack measure and 26.47% in the SME measure within a 200-query budget. Here, improvement refers to attack effectiveness, meaning greater forecast disruption. The experiments also find the examined defenses ineffective against frequency-domain manipulation, identifying a robustness problem for forecasting systems deployed behind restricted-access interfaces.
icml-2026-tsfadv-frequency-guided-black-.tldr: TSFAdv uses frequency-guided black-box queries to disrupt long-term forecasts and measures attacks through trajectory shape and directional error.

paragraphs: A pretrained language model's validation loss does not fully describe how well it will adapt to later tasks. This paper studies model plasticity: the ability to benefit from additional training. It focuses on weight decay during pretraining and asks how that choice affects the model after downstream fine-tuning.

Systematic experiments show that larger weight decay increases plasticity and produces larger downstream performance gains. This can reverse the ordering suggested by pretraining results: a base model that initially performs worse can become the better model after further training. The finding matters because tuning exclusively for base-model validation loss can miss configurations that adapt more successfully.

The authors also investigate mechanisms associated with this effect. Weight decay encourages linearly separable representations, regularizes attention matrices, and reduces overfitting to training data. Together, these observations connect one pretraining hyperparameter to several aspects of later learning. The results support including downstream adaptability when evaluating pretraining choices, alongside the cross-entropy loss of the base model.
icml-2026-weight-decay-improves-language.tldr: Larger pretraining weight decay improves downstream adaptability in experiments, sometimes allowing worse base models to become better fine-tuned models.
